newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FOCUS - Irish markets shrug off election outcome.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Irish markets shrug off election outcome.

text.p: Irish financial markets largely shrugged off the election of a centre-right minority government at the weekend, taking direction on Monday instead from international events.
Economists said that financial markets were wary but not overly perturbed by the new government's lack of a majority in parliament.

The centre-right opposition of Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrat alliance fell two seats short of a majority, holding 81 out of 166 seats. They will need the backing of independents to control parliament.
The shape and make-up of the new government will not be known until parliament sits on June 26 to elect a new prime minister, which is certain to be Ahern, analysts said.
"The outcome of the election is marginally negative but we are seeing a muted reaction to it in the markets," Riada economist Padhraic Garvey said.

"The main positive is that we have a right leaning administration in office but the negatives are that the Progressive Democrats lost a lot of seats and they were looking for a mandate to cut government spending," he said.

"Currency movements are broadly ignoring the election result," AIB Capital Markets economist Pat O'Sullivan said. He said the Irish pound was tracking sterling's gyrations against the mark in the opening session and did not appear to be overly concerned about the election outcome.
Some economists felt a majority government might have tightened fiscal policy. This would have been a bonus but they said the economy was sufficienty robust to ease their concerns.
"In an ideal world we might see a tightening of fiscal policy, but with the economy doing so well at least we can see that tax cuts etc will easily be financed," Ulster Bank economist Eoin Fahy said.
Fahy said the new government's policy was largely in line with those of its predecessor and unlikely to cause undue concern.
"I do not see the new government leading to a change in policy," he said.

Riada's Garvey said the Irish bond market was one of the poorest performers in Europe last week. There was a belief that a positive outcome to the election would have sparked some relief trade on Monday.

"If there was a positive election outcome it was expected to boost trade but that is now unlikely as the outcome was not very positive for the market. This means the underperformance we saw last week may not be clawed back."

The Irish bond market was performing in line with Europe in early trade, dealers said. The benchmark bond, due 2001, was up a quarter point at 115.55 and the bond due 2008 added 17 pence to 108.92 by 0846 GMT.
Some economists voiced concern about a minority government being vulnerable to being voted out of office, but most expected the Fianna Fail/PD alliance to last two to five years.

Speaking to Irish radio, Ahern said: "We are going to look for stability in the longer term. But at this stage I do not know the views of any of the independents. We have to get an arrangement that will last in the longer term. The aim will be to have a four or five year government."
